newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives, Labour argue over spending costs.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives, Labour argue over spending costs.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government said on Tuesday it estimated the cost of what it said were 89 public spending pledges by the opposition Labour Party at 30 billion pounds ($48.4 billion).
Labour reacted quickly to the claim, the latest move in campaigning for an election due in May, dismissing it as a "pack of lies."
William Waldegrave, chief secretary to the Treasury, told reporters the 89 spending pledges would increase public spending by 30 billion pounds each year by the end of a Labour government.
"Labour would like people to believe they have refuted each of the 89 pledges. In fact Labour have done nothing to withdraw these commitments," he said.
Labour, up to 20 points ahead in the polls, are hot favourites to win the election.
The Conservatives produced a document listing what they said were Labour spending plans.

Three of the most expensive were the restoration of public ownership of the railways, which the Conservatives reckon will cost 920 million pounds each year, 2.6 billion pounds on extra house building and 3.7 billion pounds the Conservatives say it would cost to introduce a national minimum wage.
"It is clear that in spite of their best efforts, Labour just cannot help themselves," Waldegrave said.

Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has promised to stick to Conservative spending plans for the first two years of a Labour government. Waldegrave said there was a 12 billion pound "black hole" in the claim. "But that would merely be the first instalment."

Labour dismissed the Tory claims as lies, misrepresentations or miscalculations. Party leader Tony Blair noted the launch of a new Conservative campaign poster, headlined "Tony and Bill," which flagged Labour's "30 billion pounds bill."
Addressing a number of women's groups, Blair said there was no hidden Labour spending plan. "We meet on the day the Tories launch a new poster, lying about the Labour Party.
"If there is one thing the Tories should have learned from Wirral South, it is that the public are sick of their lies, tired of the negative campaigning and want a positive vision," he said.
A by-election held last Thursday in the prosperous northern constituency of Wirral South saw a 17 percent swing to Labour, whose candidate Ben Chapman secured a majority of 7,888 votes.
Labour's rebuttal document dealt with the Conservative claims one by one.

It said its house building programme would be funded by releasing existing receipts held by local authorities, while a minimum wage would save money by cutting benefits now paid to people who are in work but poorly paid. ($ = 0.619 British Pounds)
